titre: Haymarket: eight convicted, and no one for the bomb
accroche: Chicago, 1886: eight men are tried over a bomb whose thrower remains unknown. On June 26, 1893, Governor Altgeld pardons three of them, with a written case.
contenu_vulgarise:
On the evening of May 4, 1886, in Chicago, 800 to 1,000 people, almost all of them workers, gather in Haymarket Square to protest police violence that occurred during the strikes for the eight-hour day. The rally is peaceful; the mayor, who came to listen, has left. When police advance to disperse those who remain, a bomb explodes. It wounds many and kills several policemen, including Mathias Degan. No one knows who threw it.

Eight men are indicted for Degan's murder: August Spies, Albert Parsons, Louis Lingg, Michael Schwab, Samuel Fielden, George Engel, Adolph Fischer and Oscar Neebe. All are found guilty. Seven are sentenced to hang, Neebe to fifteen years in prison. The convictions are upheld on appeal in the fall of 1887. Lingg kills himself, the sentences of Fielden and Schwab are commuted to life in prison, and Parsons, Fischer, Engel and Spies are hanged on November 11, 1887.

## Convicted for words

Judge Joseph Gary said it himself, in refusing a new trial, according to the pardon message that quotes him: the conviction does not rest on any personal participation in the act that killed Degan. It rests on the idea that the defendants had advised, by speech and in print, large categories of people to commit murder, and that someone unknown had thrown the bomb under the influence of that advice. The judge adds that the case is unprecedented: no example in the law books.

## The pardon of June 26, 1893

On June 26, 1893, the governor of Illinois, John Peter Altgeld, grants a full and unconditional pardon to Fielden, Neebe and Schwab. His message does not plead for pity. He first sets aside the argument of those who ask for clemency because the prisoners have supposedly paid enough: if the trial was fair and nothing has since shown that they were not guilty, he writes in essence, no executive intervention is justified. He therefore examines the record.

On the jury, he notes that the judge appointed a special bailiff, Henry L. Ryce, charged with summoning the men he chose, instead of drawing names by lot from a box. This, Altgeld writes, gives the bailiff absolute power to assemble a jury favorable to one side. He also cites a man who swears he heard Ryce state that the defendants would be hanged. On the evidence, he writes that the State never discovered who threw the bomb and that nothing establishes a link between the defendants and that man. Judge Gary himself wrote, in a magazine article, that it is probably true that Rudolph Schnaubelt threw it: a guess, Altgeld replies, that is not enough to convict eight men. On the judge's conduct, he writes that the complaints seem borne out by the record, but that he considers it unnecessary to discuss them further.

The pardon is then used against him. He loses his reelection bid in 1896.

## The shift

What we remember of Haymarket is a bomb and a crackdown. The 1893 record says something more precise: in 1886, the judge accepted convicting for an act without having found who committed it, provided the accused were linked to it by their words, and it is that link that the governor judged unproven in 1893. What is a link established by speeches worth when the author of the deed has never been identified?

repere.texte: On June 26, 1893, Illinois governor John P. Altgeld grants a full and unconditional pardon to Fielden, Neebe and Schwab, writing that the State never discovered who threw the Haymarket bomb and that the evidence shows no connection between the defendants and the man who threw it.
repere.source: John P. Altgeld, Reasons for Pardoning Fielden, Neebe & Schwab, the Haymarket Anarchists, June 26, 1893

carte.punch: Eight men convicted for a bomb whose thrower was never found.
carte.idee: After Haymarket (Chicago, 1886), eight men are tried for a bomb whose thrower remains unknown. In 1893, Governor Altgeld pardons the three imprisoned survivors: the evidence establishes no link with the man who threw it.

quiz.question: Why, according to Altgeld, does the evidence not show the guilt of the three men he pardons?
choix: Because he judges that they have served a sufficient sentence and that clemency is called for
Because the prosecution never identified the bomb thrower or established a link between him and the defendants
Because the real bomb thrower confessed in 1893 and cleared the defendants
Because an appeals court had overturned the conviction before his decision to pardon
quiz.explication: Altgeld expressly sets aside the argument of time already served. He writes that the State never discovered who threw the bomb, and that nothing links the defendants to that man. No confession by the real thrower is cited, and the convictions had been upheld on appeal in the fall of 1887.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what basis did Judge Gary justify the conviction of the eight defendants, according to the pardon message?
choix: Their proven personal participation in throwing the bomb
Having advised by their words murders that an unknown man supposedly committed under their influence
The defendants' refusal to testify before the jury during the trial
Their acknowledged membership in a group that had publicly claimed the attack
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Judge Gary writes that he convicted the defendants for having advised, by speech and in print, murders that an unknown man supposedly committed under that influence, not for any personal act.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what specific point does Altgeld criticize the selection of the jury?
choix: The judge appointed a special bailiff in charge of choosing the jurors
The jury was recruited solely from among employees of the McCormick factory
The jurors were questioned under oath by the police before the trial
The number of jurors was reduced from twelve to six for the trial
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Altgeld notes that the judge appointed the bailiff Ryce to summon the jurors himself, rather than drawing their names by lot from a box, giving him the power to assemble a jury favorable to the prosecution.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the identification of Rudolph Schnaubelt as a possible bomb thrower based on?
choix: An official Chicago police report filed at the trial
The sworn testimony of the bailiff Henry Ryce before the jury
A magazine article by Judge Gary, which Altgeld calls a mere guess
A signed confession obtained after his arrest by the police
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Judge Gary wrote in a magazine article that it was probably true that Schnaubelt had thrown the bomb, which Altgeld calls a mere guess, insufficient to convict eight men.
